question: Is a heavier padel racket associated with more upper-body injuries in amateur players?
reference_answer: Yes: in a survey of 950 amateur players, using a racket of 350 g or more was associated with the appearance of upper-body injuries (an association, not proven cause); shape, core, overgrips and composition were not.
agent_answer: Yes, in a study of amateur padel players, a racket weight equal to or greater than 350 g was found to be related to the appearance of injuries [munoz2022 p.5]. Specifically, the appearance of injuries is greater among amateur players when using a racket weight of 350 g or more, alongside factors such as playing more than six hours a week [munoz2022 p.7]. Tendon and muscular injuries—particularly affecting the elbow and shoulder—are the most common in this population [munoz2022 p.7]. Players experiencing persistent pain or injuries should consult a physiotherapist or doctor.

question: What injury incidence rates does the systematic review of padel injuries report?
reference_answer: 3 injuries per 1000 hours of padel training and 8 injuries per 1000 matches, with an overall prevalence of 40%-95%.
agent_answer: In their systematic review of eight studies including 2022 participants, Dahmen et al. (2023) report an incidence rate of 3 injuries per 1,000 hours of padel training and 8 injuries per 1,000 matches of padel practice [dahmen2023 p.1]. They note that these findings are based on limited literature [dahmen2023 p.1]. The review also found an overall injury prevalence ranging from 40% to 95% [dahmen2023 p.1].

This study aimed to systematically review the Method A literature search was performed up to December 2022 through MEDLINE Ovid, PubMed, Cochrane Library, SportsDiscus and CINAHL. Following database search, article retrieval and title and abstract screening, articles were assessed for eligibility against predefined criteria. Studies were assessed for methodological quality. Data on injuries’ prevalence, incidence and nature of injuries were extracted, analysed and described in a descriptive statistical manner which did not include a pooling strategy as part of a formal metaanalysis. Results Eight studies with 2022 participants were included (range of mean age: 31–57). The incidence rate was 3 injuries per 1000 hours of padel training and 8 injuries per 1000 matches of padel practice. The overall prevalence range was 40%–95%. question: Why might padel players get so many elbow tendon injuries according to the systematic review?
reference_answer: Possible reasons: many overhead shots and repetitive movements, continuous eccentric contractions when slowing the incoming ball, a stringless racket so tension is not regulated, and rare double-handed backhands.
agent_answer: According to the systematic review, the high incidence of elbow tendon injuries (such as common extensor tendinopathy or tennis elbow) may be due to the specific nature of the sport, which involves repetitive movements, a high number of overhead shots, and continuous eccentric contractions occurring after hitting the ball to slow down incoming ball speed as a tactical maneuver [dahmen2023 p.8]. If a player is experiencing persistent elbow pain, they should consult a physiotherapist or doctor for a proper evaluation.

question: How did the researchers measure where the sweet spot of a padel racket is?
reference_answer: A robot hit the racket 90 times along its central line (from 40 to 220 mm from the top, 2 mm steps, repeated three times) while an accelerometer at the handle measured vibration; the sweet spot is where the vibration severity V is minimum.
agent_answer: Researchers measured the sweet spot (SSP) by using a robot to hit padel rackets at different points along their central line with high precision, while holding the racket in a cradle that approximates a player's hand-hold [blanes2023 p.2]. They quantified the severity of each impact using accelerometers attached to the cradle's clamp at the bottom of the handle, identifying the sweet spot as the point where the impact generated the minimum reaction over the grip (the lowest vibration/V value) [blanes2023 p.2, p.7].

question: How is racket shape linked to playing style and which shapes do male and female amateurs prefer?
reference_answer: Diamond rackets tend to have higher balance (attack/power), round lower balance (control/defence), teardrop in between, though shape is less important than the physical features; men prefer diamond and women round rackets.
agent_answer:
Traditionally, racket shapes are linked to playing styles through mass distribution: diamond shapes offer a higher balance favoring power shots for attacking players, round shapes provide a lower balance for control shots suited to defensive players, and teardrop shapes occupy a polyvalent range [blanes2023 p.11-12]. 

In a survey of amateur players, shape preferences differed significantly between sexes [munoz2022 p.4, p.7]. Male amateurs tended to use more diamond-shaped rackets (35.9%), alongside teardrop (39.7%) and round (24.4%), aligning with a more aggressive style of play closer to the net [munoz2022 p.4, p.7]. In contrast, female amateurs predominantly preferred round-shaped rackets (44.2%), followed by teardrop (33.3%) and diamond (22.4%), corresponding to a more conservative game from the middle and back of the court [munoz2022 p.4, p.7].
